description: Level III prep for North Charleston repair yards, NDT labs and gauging firms facing class, UR Z17, Navy and owner audits. Send us your audit scope.
h1: Maritime NDT Consulting & Class Audit Support in North Charleston
html:
This page is for North Charleston ship repair yards, NDT subcontractors and thickness-gauging firms that have a class society, government or ship-owner audit of their NDT on the calendar. Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III consulting: we review or rebuild the written practice, the procedures and the personnel records, run a mock audit against the checklist the auditor will use, and help you answer findings with real evidence. To start, send us the audit notice or checklist and we will tell you what we need to see.

A repair waterfront built on the old Navy yard

Much of North Charleston's maritime work happens on ground the Navy once ran. The Charleston Naval Shipyard ceased operations in 1996 as a result of the 1993 base realignment round, but its basins stayed in use. Detyens Shipyards took a long-term lease and works the site with three dry docks, a floating dock and six piers, repairing military, commercial and cruise ships. A yard that handles that range of hulls cannot run a single-customer NDT program, and the firms that support it cannot either.

Another part of the former base became a federal complex with government and military tenants. Military Sealift Command roll-on/roll-off ships, Coast Guard national security cutters and NOAA research vessels berth there, and construction of a larger Coast Guard shore base on the property began in 2024. At the south end, Palmetto Railways is building an intermodal container transfer facility to connect rail with the port. Within a few miles of riverfront you find classed commercial repair work, federal contract work and heavy port construction, all drawing on one regional pool of welders, fitters and NDT technicians.

That shared pool is where audit trouble usually starts. The Level II who gauges a bulk carrier's deck plating on Monday may perform magnetic particle testing on a cutter's machinery foundation on Wednesday, under a different procedure, a different acceptance standard and a different set of records. A program written around the earliest customer tends to show gaps when the second and third customers audit it.

Who audits NDT on this waterfront, and against what

Before any document work, we map each kind of job you do to the body that sets its NDT requirements and the person who will audit it. For a typical North Charleston firm, the map looks like this.

Type of workWhere the NDT requirement comes fromWho checks itWhat they ask to see
Steel renewal and weld repair on classed commercial shipsThe ship's class rules and the yard's accepted proceduresThe attending class surveyor and the yard's quality departmentQualified personnel, an approved procedure, the agreed NDT extent and a report the surveyor can accept
Thickness measurement credited to a class surveyIACS UR Z17 plus the society's own service supplier schemeThe society's approval auditor, then the surveyor on each jobA current Certificate of Approval from that society, qualified operators, a named supervisor, calibrated gauges and the approved report format
Repairs on government hulls under federal contractsThe contract and the technical publications it referencesThe government's quality representative and any prime contractorA written practice, procedures and certification records that match the contract wording
Owner, charterer and pre-purchase gaugingThe owner's or buyer's specificationThe superintendent or the buyer's surveyorEvidence of competence, traceable reading locations and an independent report
Port, rail and terminal constructionThe project specification and the structural welding code it names, often AWS D1.1The owner's inspector or engineer of recordA written practice, a code-compliant procedure and certified inspectors

The point of the map is to stop one set of documents from pretending to serve every customer. Most firms need one written practice that covers all of their work, with method procedures that say which acceptance standard applies to which customer, and job instructions that pull the right one. An auditor from any of these bodies should be able to trace a single job from the purchase order to the procedure, the technician's certification and the signed report without help. For the structural work on the port side, our AWS D1.1 compliance page covers what that code expects from NDT personnel.

Class approval audits for gauging firms that serve Charleston ships

Ships that come to North Charleston for dry docking often have a class survey due at the same time, and steel renewal decisions on those surveys rest on thickness readings. When the readings are credited to a class survey, IACS UR Z17 requires the firm taking them to hold approval from that ship's class society. The approval belongs to the company and names one society; a certificate from one does not carry over to another. Thickness measurement firms renew at intervals of no more than three years, which is shorter than the five-year limit for most other supplier categories.

The society's process runs in a fixed order: a document submission, an audit of the office to confirm the firm works the way its documents say, and a witnessed practical demonstration with a satisfactory report. The documents include a company outline, the list of operators with their training, experience and qualifications, the equipment and its calibration records, training programmes, checklists, report formats and a quality manual. The full requirement set is broken down in our IACS service supplier approval guide and on the UR Z17 compliance page, so this page does not repeat it.

What we see go wrong for gauging firms in the Southeast is less about the rules and more about the evidence. Operator files carry a certificate number but no record of the supervised field work behind it. The supervisor named on the application has not actually reviewed a report in months. The gauge was calibrated, but nobody kept the step-block readings taken on the job. Each of those becomes a finding because the auditor cannot see what the document claims. The UTM operator qualification work we do fixes the personnel side before anything else, because it takes the longest to evidence.

Weld NDT on commercial repairs: what the class surveyor looks for

When a yard renews shell plating, inserts a new bulkhead section or repairs a cracked bracket on a classed ship, the class surveyor decides whether the repair is acceptable, and NDT is part of the evidence. The extent of testing comes from the society's rules and from the repair plan agreed with the surveyor. IACS Recommendation No. 20 on non-destructive testing of hull welds is the industry's shared reference for methods, extent and acceptance, and individual societies publish their own guidance on top of it.

Surveyors at repair yards tend to check a short list of things in person: that the technician holds certification in the method under a recognised scheme, that the procedure on the job is the approved revision, that the surface condition and lighting suit the method, and that the report identifies the weld well enough to find it again. If radiography is part of the plan, yards in the United States subcontract it to a licensed radiography firm; Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US, though as a Level III it can review the radiographs and the RT procedure. The paperwork that follows a repair through to the class report is described in our ship repair yard NDT program guide.

The typical findings we help yards close are practical. A subcontracted MT technician arrived without a current vision record. The UT procedure on file did not cover the plate thickness or the probe angles used. The NDT map in the repair package did not match the welds actually tested. None of these needs a new quality system; they need a written practice that is enforced, procedures that cover the actual work, and someone who checks the subcontractor's papers at the gate. A subcontractor approval audit gives the yard that gate.

Government hulls on the old base: Sealift, Coast Guard and NOAA

The federal tenants on the former base change the audit picture. Military Sealift Command ships are generally kept in class, so a repair package can involve both a class surveyor and government contract requirements at the same time. Coast Guard cutter repairs follow the technical requirements the Coast Guard writes into its own contracts. NOAA research ships bring their own specifications. In each case the contract, not habit, decides which documents govern the NDT.

Where a contract invokes NAVSEA technical publications, the NDT rules are NAVSEA's and not a class society's. NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 treats SNT-TC-1A as mandatory minimums rather than guidance, recertifies operators and inspectors by examination at least every three years, and requires each NDT procedure to be qualified and approved within the activity that uses it. A firm that has only ever worked to class rules usually needs to rewrite its written practice before that kind of audit. Our pages on NAVSEA NDT requirements for shipyards and T9074 compliance set out the differences in detail.

We do not decide for you which document applies. We read the contract clauses and referenced specifications with your quality manager, list the NDT requirements they create, and show where your current program meets them and where it does not. Your contracting officer or prime contractor confirms the reading; we make sure your documents can survive it.

What an auditor opens early in a North Charleston NDT program

Whoever the auditor is, the sequence is similar. They start with records, because records show whether the manual is real. In our mock audits we pull the same items in roughly the same order.

  • The written practice: whether it names the scheme the contract or rule requires (SNT-TC-1A or CP-189), covers every method you use, and defines training, experience, examinations, vision and recertification in a way your records actually follow.
  • Two or three technician files chosen at random: training hours, experience logs, general, specific and practical examination results, annual vision checks and the employer's certification signature.
  • Procedures and technique sheets: revision status, Level III approval, the rule or code they implement and, where required, evidence of a procedure demonstration.
  • Equipment: calibration certificates for gauges, flaw detectors and yokes, reference blocks with traceable material and dimensions, and the checks done on the job.
  • Reports from real jobs: whether each report ties back to the procedure revision, the instrument serial number and a certified person.
  • Subcontractor control: how you approve an NDT subcontractor, and the file that proves you did.
  • Corrective actions: the last few findings and the evidence that each one was closed, not just answered.

Firms that track certifications and calibration dates in spreadsheets often lose time here. An expired card or an overdue gauge found during the audit is a finding even if it was never used on a job. Our certificate tracking app exists because this is the most common avoidable finding we see, and the vision examination records service covers the paperwork side of the same problem.

How Atlantis supports firms in North Charleston

Atlantis has no office in South Carolina. We work from Houston, do most of the document work remotely, and travel to your yard or office when the job needs eyes on the floor: a mock audit, a procedure demonstration, or a review of how technicians actually set up on the job. An engagement usually runs in four stages.

  1. Scope: you send the audit notice, the auditor's checklist if you have it, and your current written practice and procedures. We confirm which requirements apply.
  2. Gap review: our Level III reads the documents against those requirements and samples your records, then gives you a list of gaps ranked by audit risk.
  3. Fix: we redraft the written practice, procedures and technique sheets for your approval, rebuild record templates, and help you gather missing evidence. Your managers approve and sign; the documents are yours.
  4. Rehearse and respond: we run a mock audit on site or by video, and after the real audit we help you write corrective actions with evidence the auditor will accept.

The people doing the work stay responsible for it. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its own personnel. The class society decides on approval, and the government representative decides on contract compliance. Atlantis is the Level III adviser preparing you for those decisions, not the body making them. If you need documents written from scratch, see written practice development and procedure qualification and demonstration.

Where Atlantis stands on its own class approval

Atlantis holds no class approval today. We are working through the UR Z17 process with ABS, DNV and Lloyd's Register for our own thickness measurement services, which means our people are preparing the same document packs, office audits and practical demonstrations that we help clients prepare. We say this plainly because it affects what we can offer: we can prepare your firm for a class audit, but we cannot lend you an approval, and readings taken by Atlantis are not credited to a class survey until a society issues us a certificate.

What to send us before the kickoff call

  • The audit notice or the society's, customer's or contracting officer's checklist, and the date of the audit.
  • Your current written practice and the list of methods and levels you certify.
  • The NDT procedures and technique sheets you use for ship work, with revision dates.
  • A sample of three technician qualification files, with names removed if you prefer.
  • Your equipment list with calibration dates, and two recent job reports.
  • Any findings from previous audits and how you answered them.

We reply within one business day. If your team also needs training before the audit, our maritime NDT training and the North Charleston training page cover the options.

North Charleston audit-readiness checklist

  1. List every customer type you serve on the waterfront and the document each one names for NDT.
  2. Confirm your written practice covers every method and level you actually certify, under the scheme those customers name.
  3. Check every technician's vision record date before the audit, including subcontractors who work in the dry docks or on the federal piers.
  4. Match each method procedure to the acceptance standards it applies, and state which customer each standard belongs to.
  5. If you gauge for class surveys, confirm which societies you hold approval from and the expiry date of each certificate.
  6. Pull two recent reports and trace each one to the procedure revision, the instrument and the technician's certification.
  7. Review your NDT subcontractor files, including any licensed radiography firm you use.
  8. Close or evidence every open corrective action from the last audit.

For the national picture of maritime NDT audits, see maritime NDT audit support. Nearby ports on the South Atlantic coast have their own pages for Brunswick, Georgia and Jacksonville, and general Level III support in the area is on our North Charleston consulting page. The region's aerospace manufacturing works under a different audit regime, covered on the aerospace NDT training page.

faq.q: Does a thickness gauging firm need class approval to work on ships repaired in North Charleston?
faq.a: Only when the readings are credited to a class survey. In that case IACS UR Z17 requires approval from the ship's own class society, and each society issues its own certificate. Gauging done purely for an owner, a buyer or a charterer does not need class approval, though many buyers ask for it anyway. Our UR Z17 audit preparation page lists what the society checks.

faq.q: Can an outside Level III sign our written practice for a class approval application?
faq.a: Yes. UR Z17 accepts employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations, as long as that Level III is qualified in each method. Your company still certifies its people and keeps the records. Our Level III holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

faq.q: Do repairs on Sealift, Coast Guard or NOAA ships at the former Navy base follow class rules?
faq.a: Not by default. The contract decides. A Sealift ship kept in class can bring a class surveyor into the job, a Coast Guard contract carries the Coast Guard's own requirements, and any contract that invokes NAVSEA technical publications puts NDT under NAVSEA rules rather than class rules. We help you read the clauses; the contracting officer confirms them.

faq.q: We subcontract radiography on ship repairs. What will the auditor want to see?
faq.a: A subcontractor approval file: the radiography firm's radioactive materials license, its written practice, the RT procedure it will use, certification and vision records for the radiographers, and evidence that you reviewed all of it before the job. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US, but our Level III can review the film or digital images and the RT procedure. See subcontractor approval audits.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have staff based in North Charleston?
faq.a: No. Atlantis works from Houston and Hyderabad. We handle document reviews and drafting remotely and travel to North Charleston for site work such as mock audits, procedure demonstrations and floor observations.

faq.q: Can the mock audit be done by video?
faq.a: The records part can. We review your written practice, procedures and a sample of technician and equipment files through a shared folder and walk through them with you on a call. Watching technicians set up and test on a real weld or plate needs a site visit, and we plan that visit around your production schedule.

faq.q: Will Atlantis speak to the class society for us during the approval?
faq.a: Your company stays the applicant and the society deals with you. If you want, our Level III can attend the office audit or the practical demonstration as your adviser and help answer technical questions about the written practice and procedures. The society makes the approval decision.

faq.q: Does Atlantis write welding procedures for the yard?
faq.a: No. Welding procedure specifications and their qualification records belong to the yard and its welding engineer. Atlantis confines its work to the NDT side. For background on how welding procedures are qualified, see our WPS, PQR and WPQ guide.

faq.q: Does Atlantis hold class approval itself?
faq.a: Not yet. Atlantis is going through the UR Z17 process with ABS, DNV and Lloyd's Register for its own thickness measurement services and has no class approval today. Until a society issues a certificate, readings taken by Atlantis are not credited to class surveys.

faq.q: What should we fix if our audit date is close?
faq.a: Start with the items an auditor can verify in minutes: expired certifications, missing vision records, gauges past calibration, and procedures on the floor that do not match the approved revision. Those are quick to find and quick to fix. Rewriting a written practice takes longer, so if it needs work, tell the auditor what is in progress rather than presenting an unapproved draft.
